title: ASIC warns brokers over loan advice
full_text:
In more than one out of five home loan recommendations, mortgage brokers are passing over the cheapest deal, and the corporate regulator says many are failing to adequately explain why.
An Australian Securities and Investments Commission audit of the largest aggregator groups, which provide services to about 27,800 mortgage brokers, found compliance with their "best interest duty" obligations could be improved, including closer monitoring of broker fees and increasing resources to handle borrower complaints.
The "best interest duty" called for by the Hayne royal commission's final report in 2019 requires brokers to act in the customer's best interests when recommending a home loan.
ASIC said seven of the eight aggregators it reviewed reported that brokers did not recommend the cheapest loan option in more than 20 per cent of cases. It found instances where "brokers did not have clear evidence to support those recommendations".
"Obviously, in the context of cost-of-living concerns, price will be a major factor for many consumers and price also goes to the core of the best interest duty," ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said. "Features are part of the assessment, but price is obviously the dominant factor."
ASIC's warning comes amid intensifying competition for business in the mortgage market as house prices fall on the back of rising official interest rates.
Still, the regulator found no evidence of brokers actively putting customers into inappropriate loans or favouring lenders who paid higher commissions, and said the sector was mostly aligned with its best practice guidance, known as RG273.
This states it is unlikely to be in the borrower's best interests for a broker to suggest they apply for a loan if there is a cheaper loan the broker could recommend that would meet the consumer's non-cost objectives. These could include access to offset accounts or redraw facilities, approval times, lender preference such as brand or reputation, and the need for a special assessment if a borrower has non-standard income sources.
Mortgage & Finance Association of Australia chief executive Anja Pannek said ASIC had provided a road map for brokers, aggregators and licensees to strengthen practices and consumer outcomes.
"Price absolutely matters. Consumers should have confidence that their broker has considered the available options, and can clearly explain why a particular loan is in their best interests," she said. "At the same time, the lowest-cost loan is not necessarily the right loan for every borrower."
The existence of the best interest duty has helped brokers continue to win over customers: brokers arranged a record level of mortgages, more than 81 per cent of the nationwide total, or 838,815 loans, worth $495 billion in 2025.
The major aggregators examined by ASIC were: Australian Finance Group, Lendi, Loan Market, Mortgage Choice, Finsure, Connective, Yellow Brick Road and Outsource Financial.
ASIC examined data up to March last year, with many operators lifting investment in their systems over the past 18 months since the audit was completed.
"Aggregators sit at the centre of the mortgage broking system, so they should be able to allow ASIC to see what's actually happening in lending through brokers," Kirkland said.
"But they themselves should also be looking at that data so they can understand where there might be risks involving particular brokers or groups of brokers."
ASIC said it supported the greater use of artificial intelligence but noted that investment in the technology needed to be accompanied by strong data management, controls and governance. "Outputs from any decision tools or AI agents should be explainable and documented, including the relevant data used to create them," the regulator said.
Scrutiny on the best interest duty comes as ASIC has put the entire mortgage origination chain on notice by including heightened scrutiny of bank referrer programs and remuneration in its 2026-27 supervisory agenda.
"Mortgage payments will be the most significant expense that any Australian household that has a mortgage will be paying, so we want to understand how mortgages are being approved, what advice is being provided as part of that process, and what the outcomes are for consumers," said Kirkland.
ASIC also found evidence that some broker complaints were being missed, withdrawn without being fully investigated, or delayed. It pointed to insufficient resources or a lack of information to investigate as possible causes.
Mortgage brokers still generate a small volume of complaints, representing about 5.4 per cent of the total made to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. Of these, less than 10 per cent relate to the best interests duty.
But Kirkland said ASIC needed brokers to "get the basics right for those customers who have complained as there might be a really serious reason behind that complaint, and if it is properly investigated, that might lead to a significant outcome for them."
